context: Current closing price of Southwest Airlines (LUV): $45.62 USD as of 2026-07-30.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the current market price level near $45.75. At the one-day horizon, the estimate stays essentially flat because short-term price action for most assets tends to mean-revert around recent levels absent a specific catalyst, and I had no strong directional signal to justify a meaningful move. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $46.00, reflecting a mild positive bias that could come from broader market momentum or sector tailwinds. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises further to $46.50, incorporating a small drift premium that accounts for the general tendency of risk assets to appreciate modestly over time when no major macro headwinds are evident.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons, which is standard for any forecast under uncertainty — more time means more opportunity for new information to arrive and move prices. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly $44.20 to $47.30 reflects typical intraday-to-overnight volatility, acknowledging that even a single news item or earnings revision could shift prices by 2–3%. At one week, the interval expands to $43–$49, capturing the possibility of a meaningful macro data release, central bank commentary, or sector-specific development. At one month, the $40–$53 band is intentionally wide because a full month encompasses multiple potential catalysts, earnings cycles, and macro events that could cumulatively shift the price by 10–15% in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals entirely. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — particularly inflation or employment figures that shift central bank expectations — could trigger a broad risk-off selloff well beyond my lower bounds. Geopolitical escalation or a credit event in a systemically important institution could also produce tail moves larger than my intervals imply. On the upside, a surprise positive earnings beat, an unexpected rate cut signal, or a sector-specific catalyst such as a merger announcement could push prices sharply above $53 within a month.

Finally, I should be transparent that these estimates carry model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. I do not have real-time data access, so my starting price assumption may itself be slightly off, which would shift the entire distribution. My intervals are best interpreted as indicative ranges under normal market conditions rather than hard bounds, and fat-tail events — which occur more frequently than Gaussian models suggest — remain a persistent source of risk that my stated 90% intervals likely understate in practice.
